title: Hopi Mythology: Figures, Relationships and Story Cycles
description: The Hopi world mapped as a relationship graph: the emergence through the sipapu, Masauwu and the short ear of corn, Spider Grandmother and the war twins, and the katsinam who live at the villages for half of every year.
sources: H. R. Voth, The Traditions of the Hopi (1905) - the largest single collection of recorded Hopi narrative
J. W. Fewkes, Hopi Katcinas Drawn by Native Artists (1903) - the katsina figures, drawn by Hopi artists
J. W. Fewkes, Tusayan Migration Traditions (1900)
H. R. Voth, The Oraibi Summer Snake Ceremony (1903)
Note: the popular Taiowa and Sotuknang creation account comes from Frank Waters, Book of the Hopi (1963), which is not used here and is disputed by many Hopi
portraitNote: Portraits are original illustrations, never photographs of carved tithu or of ceremonies. Drawn in a single uniform style for the whole pack, stored locally in the portraits/hopi/ folder. No images are fetched from the network.

profile.cosmicNature: Four worlds, stacked. People climbed up out of each one when it went bad, through a hole called the sipapu, and we are living in the fourth. The first three ended because people forgot how to behave, not because of any flood or fire sent from outside. There is a way out of this one too, and everybody knows roughly where it is.
profile.natureOfDivinity: Not a pantheon so much as a crowd of relatives. Tawa the sun, Masauwu who owns this world, Spider Grandmother who fixes things, and several hundred katsinam - spirits of rain, corn, animals and the dead who come and live at the villages for half the year and then go home. The gods are neighbours, and they are expected to show up.
profile.afterlife: You go west, to the San Francisco Peaks or down through the sipapu, and if you lived well you come back as a cloud. That is not a metaphor. The dead return as rain, which is the entire point in a place that gets ten inches of it a year.
profile.systemMechanism: Reciprocity, and a bargain with the hardest land in North America. Masauwu offered the Hopi a short ear of corn and a hard life at Oraibi, and they took it on purpose. Ceremony is the work of holding up the year: get the dances right, keep a good heart, and the rain comes. Get it wrong and it does not.
profile.canonTexts: There is no book. The material below was recorded from Hopi narrators between 1890 and 1905 by H. R. Voth and J. W. Fewkes and printed by the Field Museum and the Bureau of American Ethnology. Different villages tell it differently, and the versions here are the ones that got written down.

hierarchy.title: The Makers
hierarchy.blurb: The sun, a woman who lives in the sea, and a small spider who is better at everything than anyone. Between them they make the world and the people in it.
hierarchy.connectorCaption: Three worlds go wrong before this one, and the people climb up through a hole

hierarchy.title: The Emergence
hierarchy.blurb: The Fourth World comes with a landlord. Masauwu lays out ears of corn and lets each people choose; the Hopi take the short blue one, and get the hardest country and the longest tenure.
hierarchy.connectorCaption: The world arrives dangerous, and two small boys are sent to clean it up

hierarchy.title: Monsters, Serpents and the Boy in the Log
hierarchy.blurb: A giant bird that takes people off the mesas, a horned serpent living in the springs, and a boy who sealed himself in a cottonwood log to find out where the river went.
hierarchy.connectorCaption: He came back with the rain rites - and the rain comes with the katsinam

hierarchy.title: The Katsinam Arrive
hierarchy.blurb: For half the year, several hundred spirits live at the villages. The chief is the plainest-looking of all of them, and the most important thing anyone does is pour water on a cloud drawn in cornmeal.
hierarchy.connectorCaption: In February the children find out what the katsinam actually are

hierarchy.title: Powamu: Whips, Ogres and Bean Sprouts
hierarchy.blurb: Beans forced green in heated kivas in the middle of winter, children whipped at their initiation, and an ogre at the door with a basket, negotiating for your son.
hierarchy.connectorCaption: And then the clowns, who exist to be everything a person should not be

hierarchy.title: Clowns and the Reckoning
hierarchy.blurb: The Koyemsi run the games and the Tsuku behave appallingly for an entire afternoon, until the owl comes down off the roof with a whip. The punishment is the second half of the lesson.
hierarchy.connectorCaption: Between them, the dances that actually ask for the rain

hierarchy.title: The Rain Dances and Going Home
hierarchy.blurb: Longhairs singing the best songs of the year, the Water Drinking Girl in the tallest headdress, eagles raised on the rooftops - and in July the first corn comes in and the katsinam leave.

stories.title: Coming Up Through the Hole
stories.summary: Three worlds before this one, and each ended the same way - people stopped behaving, the place went bad, and those who still had good hearts left. A reed was planted and grew up through the sky, and they climbed it. Coming out into the Fourth World they found it dark, cold and already owned. Masauwu was there. The world had to be made habitable before anyone could farm it: the elder twin hardened the ground, the younger sent sound through it, and the two of them went hunting the monsters that were already living here.

sources.translation: H. R. Voth, Field Columbian Museum, 1905
sources.location: The Traditions of the Hopi, I

sources.translation: J. W. Fewkes, BAE 19th Annual Report, 1900

stories.title: The Short Ear of Corn
stories.summary: At the top, Masauwu laid ears of corn on the ground and told the peoples who had come up to choose. The others went first and took the long fat ears - the easy ones, the ones that promised plenty. What was left when the Hopi came forward was a short blue ear, and they took it. That choice bought them the highest, driest, least promising country in the region, a life of hard farming, and, as it turns out, the longest continuous occupation of anywhere in North America. The whole culture reads that as a deliberate decision rather than bad luck.

sources.translation: H. R. Voth, Field Columbian Museum, 1905
J. W. Fewkes, BAE 19th Annual Report, 1900

stories.title: The Boy Who Went Down the River
stories.summary: Tiyo watched the river running away west and wanted to know where it went. His father hollowed a cottonwood log, sealed him inside with pitch and some food, and pushed it into the water. Spider Grandmother shrank herself and rode behind his ear the whole way, telling him what to do. He came at last to the Snake People, passed their tests, and married a Snake Maiden, bringing home the songs and the altar for making rain. Their first children were born as snakes and bit the village children, so the family moved on - and the snakes went into the ground.

sources.translation: H. R. Voth, Field Columbian Museum, 1903
J. W. Fewkes, BAE 19th Annual Report, 1900

stories.title: Beans in February
stories.summary: In February, when there is nothing growing anywhere, beans are planted in boxes in the kivas and the kivas are heated day and night until they come up green. Before dawn Ahola goes to every house in the village and marks it with cornmeal. Eototo walks the plaza at a deliberate pace, stopping to draw clouds on the ground and pour water on them. Crow Mother carries in the sprouts. The whole thing is a demonstration, in the deadest part of the year, that growth is still available - and an argument, addressed to whoever is listening, that it should continue.

sources.translation: H. R. Voth, Field Columbian Museum, 1905

sources.book: Hopi Katcinas Drawn by Native Artists
sources.translation: J. W. Fewkes, BAE 21st Annual Report, 1903

stories.title: What the Children Find Out
stories.summary: Children are initiated at around eight or nine. Crow Mother brings the yucca whips into the kiva and the Hu katsinam use them, four strokes each, and it is not symbolic. Then, at the end, the katsinam take off their masks - and the children see their own uncles and neighbours underneath. Hopi people who have written about that moment describe the shock of it, and then something larger: not that it was a trick, but that the katsinam are genuinely present in the men who carry them. It is the point at which a child stops being an audience and starts being responsible.

sources.translation: H. R. Voth, Field Columbian Museum, 1905

stories.title: The Ogres Come for the Children
stories.summary: Soyoko goes house to house with a basket and a knife, naming specific children and demanding them. The Natacka stand behind her clacking enormous wooden beaks. The child has to come out and face her. The family bargains - offering food instead of the child, while the child promises to work harder and behave - and she refuses, and comes back, and the price goes up over several visits until she is finally bought off with meat. The children are genuinely frightened. The adults are visibly enjoying themselves. It is the most effective piece of parenting anyone has ever written down.

sources.translation: H. R. Voth, Field Columbian Museum, 1905

sources.book: Hopi Katcinas Drawn by Native Artists
sources.translation: J. W. Fewkes, BAE 21st Annual Report, 1903

stories.title: The Clowns Go Too Far
stories.summary: The clowns come down into the plaza backwards and spend the day being everything a person should not be - eating enormously, drinking filthy water, mocking the audience by name, imitating the visitors, getting worse as the hours pass. Everyone can feel where it is going. Then the warriors and Mongwu the great horned owl appear on the rooftops, watch for a while, and come down. The clowns are drenched, thrashed with yucca whips and made to apologise. The excess and the correction are two halves of one argument, delivered over an entire afternoon to the whole village at once.

stories.title: The Home Dance
stories.summary: In July the Hemis katsinam bring in the first green corn of the year and it is given out. Girls who married that season receive their wedding robes. The Longhairs sing, and the songs are new that year and by common agreement the best of the cycle. Then it is over: the katsinam leave the villages and go back to the San Francisco Peaks for six months, and the eagles raised on the rooftops through the summer are sent home too. The dance is called Niman, which means going home, and it is the most beautiful thing in the calendar because it is the end of it.

sources.book: Hopi Katcinas Drawn by Native Artists
sources.translation: J. W. Fewkes, BAE 21st Annual Report, 1903
H. R. Voth, Field Columbian Museum, 1905

entities.name: Tawa
entities.role: The sun, who made the world and still crosses it twice a day
symbols: the disc face ringed with feathers and a fox skin
entities.bio: The sun god, who leaves his eastern house every morning and gets to the western one by evening.
entities.longBio: Tawa is the sun and the maker. In the Hopi telling he does not sit above the world issuing orders; he travels it, every single day, east house to west house, and the whole year is organised around watching exactly where on the horizon he comes up. The Sun Watcher's job was to call the ceremonies by that mark, and getting it wrong meant planting at the wrong time. His face in the art is a disc ringed with eagle feathers and red horsehair. Children are presented to him at dawn on their twentieth day and given their name.
entities.variantTraditions: Some accounts pair him with Spider Grandmother as co-creator; the popular version with Taiowa and Sotuknang above him comes from a 1963 book, not from the older recorded material.

entities.name: Spider Grandmother
entities.role: The small one who fixes everything, and rides behind your ear
symbols: the small hole in the ground
entities.abode: A hole in the ground, which is much bigger inside
entities.bio: The most useful being in Hopi story: she makes people out of clay, and turns up whenever anyone is stuck.
entities.longBio: Spider Grandmother lives in an unremarkable hole in the ground that turns out to be a whole house inside. She is the one who moulds the first people from clay and sings over them, and after that her role is essentially technical support - a hero in trouble hears a small voice, looks down, and there she is. Her standard move is to shrink herself and ride along behind the traveller's ear, giving directions. She is never grand and never wrong, and she is easily the most affectionately told figure in the whole record.
entities.variantTraditions: She appears across the Pueblo and Navajo traditions in closely related roles, which makes her one of the most widespread figures in the Southwest.

entities.name: Masauwu
entities.role: Owner of this world, god of death and fire, and the ugliest thing you will ever meet
epithets: the owner of the Fourth World
entities.abode: The edges of the fields, and the road at night
entities.bio: He owns the world we live on, met the Hopi when they emerged, and offered them the shortest ear of corn on purpose.
entities.longBio: Masauwu is terrifying to look at - a great bald head, blood on the face, and he carries fire - and he is not the villain. He owns the Fourth World, and when the people came up out of the sipapu he laid out ears of corn and let each group choose. The others grabbed the long fat ones. The Hopi took the short blue one last, which meant a hard life, little rain, and survival. That choice is the founding decision of the whole culture. He also walks the fields at night and is the one you meet at the boundary between the living and the dead.
entities.variantTraditions: His name is written Masauwu, Maasaw and Masau'u across sources. He is simultaneously a death god and a friendly figure to farmers, which the ethnographers found confusing and the Hopi did not.

entities.name: Muyingwa
entities.role: God of germination, who lives underground and pushes the seed up
entities.bio: The one who makes seeds decide to grow, which in a place with ten inches of rain is the whole game.
entities.longBio: Muyingwa lives underground and is responsible for the moment a seed cracks and pushes. Hopi farming is dry farming - no irrigation, corn planted a foot deep in sand to reach buried moisture - so germination is not a given, and Muyingwa is petitioned hard. He is closely tied to the four coloured corns, blue, white, red and yellow, and to the Powamu ceremony in February, where bean plants are forced in heated kivas and brought out green in the middle of winter as proof the year will work.
entities.variantTraditions: Some villages call the germination deity Alosaka and pair him with Muyingwa; the relationship between the two names varies by mesa.

entities.name: Hard Beings Woman
entities.role: The woman who owns all hard things - shell, coral, turquoise - and lives out at sea
symbols: the kiva ladder rising from the water
entities.abode: A kiva in the middle of the water, east and west
entities.bio: There are two of her, one in the eastern ocean and one in the western, and she owns everything hard and precious.
entities.longBio: In Voth's creation account the Hard Beings Woman is there at the start with Tawa. She lives in a kiva out in the water, reached by a ladder, and she owns all the hard beautiful substances - turquoise, coral, shell, beads. She and the sun make the first people together. Then the eastern and western ones consult and decide there should be dry land in between, which is how the world gets made. She is an odd, memorable figure: a goddess of the sea and of jewellery, in a culture living in a high desert five hundred miles from any ocean.
entities.variantTraditions: The name is also written Huruing Wuhti. That a landlocked people put their creator goddess in the middle of the sea is one of the strongest hints of very old contact and trade routes to the Pacific.

entities.name: Poqanghoya
entities.role: The elder war twin, who hardened the earth so people could walk on it
entities.bio: Half of the pair of small violent boys who make the world safe by killing everything dangerous in it.
entities.longBio: Poqanghoya and his younger brother are Spider Grandmother's grandsons, and they are children - they play games, they are cheeky to their grandmother, they get told off. They are also the ones sent to make the world liveable: the elder solidifies the earth, which had been soft and unstable, and between them they hunt down and kill the monsters that made the Fourth World dangerous. In the ceremonies they are the war twins, and their images are set out to guard. Small boys as the most dangerous beings in the world is a Southwestern speciality.
entities.variantTraditions: The twins recur through Pueblo and Navajo tradition, and their names shift between villages. They are sometimes said to sit at the north and south poles keeping the earth steady.

entities.name: Palongawhoya
entities.role: The younger war twin, who sent sound through the world and kept it echoing
entities.bio: His job was sound: he sent it out through the world and it has not stopped bouncing since.
entities.longBio: The younger of Spider Grandmother's grandsons. Where his brother makes the earth solid, Palongawhoya's assignment is sound - he carries it out through the world so that the whole thing resonates, and echo is what is left of that. The pair of them then go monster-hunting. They are simultaneously the guardians invoked in serious ceremony and a pair of badly behaved boys who cannot be left alone with anything, and the stories enjoy both. In modern retellings the sound-carrying job has been romanticised considerably; the older accounts are blunter about it.
entities.variantTraditions: The elaborate vibration cosmology attached to him in some popular books comes from Frank Waters (1963) rather than from the earlier recorded material.

entities.name: The Sipapu
entities.role: The hole people climbed out of, and the door the dead go back through
symbols: the reed that grew up through the sky
the round hole in the kiva floor
entities.abode: A travertine dome in the Grand Canyon, on the Little Colorado
entities.bio: Not a person - a hole. The people climbed up through it into this world, and the dead go back down the same way.
entities.longBio: The sipapu is where the Third World ended and this one started: a reed grew up through the sky and the people climbed it, and came out here. There is a physical place, a yellow travertine dome on the Little Colorado in the Grand Canyon, that is identified as it. Every kiva has a small round hole in the floor representing it, so that the room you hold ceremonies in is literally built around the door between worlds. The dead take the same road back. It is the single most important location in Hopi thought and it is a hole in the ground.
entities.variantTraditions: Related emergence traditions and physical sipapu sites are held by other Pueblo peoples and the Navajo, with different locations.

entities.name: Matsito
entities.role: The chief who founded Oraibi after a quarrel with his brother
entities.bio: He fell out with his brother, walked away, and started what became the oldest continuously inhabited settlement in North America.
entities.longBio: Matsito quarrels with his brother, the chief at Shungopavi, and leaves to found his own village on Third Mesa. That village is Oraibi, and people have lived in it since roughly 1100, which makes it a serious contender for the oldest continuously occupied settlement in the United States. He marks the boundaries of the fields and lays out who holds what. The story is a charter - it explains why Oraibi exists and why its land is divided the way it is - and it is told with the flatness of an actual property dispute.
entities.variantTraditions: Oraibi split again in 1906 in a dispute between the Friendlies and Hostiles, settled by a push-of-war across a line scratched in the rock. That line is still there.

entities.name: Tiyo
entities.role: The boy who floated down the Colorado in a hollow log to find out where the water goes
epithets: the one who went down the river
symbols: the hollow cottonwood log sealed with pitch
entities.abode: Down the river, and back to Walpi
entities.bio: He wondered where all the water went, sealed himself into a log, and went to find out.
entities.longBio: Tiyo watches the river run away west and wants to know where it ends. His father hollows a cottonwood log, seals him in with pitch and food, and pushes him off. Spider Grandmother rides along behind his ear. He reaches the Snake People, is tested, marries a Snake Maiden and brings her home with the songs and rites for making rain. Their first children are snakes, which does not go well in the village, so the family moves on. The story is the origin of the Snake Dance at Walpi, in which real rattlesnakes are carried in the mouth, and it is why.
entities.variantTraditions: Voth and Fewkes both recorded versions, differing in detail. The Snake Dance was closed to outsiders in the twentieth century after decades of intrusive tourism.

entities.name: The Snake Maiden
entities.role: Tiyo's wife from the Snake People, who brought the rain ceremony north
entities.abode: The Snake kiva, and then Walpi
entities.bio: She married the boy who came down the river in a log, and her children came out as snakes.
entities.longBio: The Snake Maiden comes back north with Tiyo, bringing the songs, the altar and the rites that make rain. Her first children are born as snakes and bite the village children, so the family leaves and settles elsewhere - and the snakes go into the ground and become the ones handled in the ceremony. That is the point: the rattlesnakes carried in the dancers' mouths at Walpi are kin. They are sent out afterwards to the four directions to carry the message that the people need rain.
entities.variantTraditions: The identification of the ceremonial snakes as relatives is explicit in the recorded accounts and is why the dance is not the daredevil stunt outsiders took it for.

entities.name: Palulukang
entities.role: The horned water serpent who lives in springs and shakes the ground
entities.abode: Springs, and the water under the ground
entities.bio: He lives in the springs, and when he moves the earth moves with him.
entities.longBio: Palulukang is the great horned serpent who inhabits the water below the ground - the springs, and whatever it is that connects them. When he shifts, there are earthquakes and floods. He is brought out in the Powamu season in a screen ceremony where puppet serpents several feet long lunge out through a painted cloth at the audience, worked from behind by men in the dark, and knock over corn plants. It is genuinely startling to watch and was described with some astonishment by every ethnographer who saw it. He is a relative of the Zuni Kolowisi and of the plumed serpents further south.
entities.variantTraditions: The horned or plumed water serpent runs from the Pueblos through Mesoamerica, and how closely Palulukang relates to Quetzalcoatl is an old and unresolved question.

entities.name: Kwatoko
entities.role: The monster bird that ate people, killed by the twins
entities.bio: A giant bird that carried people off, until two small boys went up the cliff after it.
entities.longBio: Kwatoko is one of the monsters left over in the Fourth World, a huge bird that takes people off the mesas. The war twins go after it - climbing to the eyrie, dealing with the chicks, and killing the adult - which is the standard shape of their work: the world is delivered dangerous and has to be cleaned up before it can be farmed. The monster-killing stories are told briskly and with a certain relish, and they are the reason the twins appear as guardians on altars.
entities.variantTraditions: Monster-slaying cycles of this kind are shared across the Southwest, most fully developed in the Navajo Hero Twins material.

entities.name: Mongwu
entities.role: The great horned owl, who is the one who finally disciplines the clowns
entities.abode: The night, and the edge of the plaza
entities.bio: When the clowns have gone too far, the owl arrives with a whip, and everybody knows it was coming.
entities.longBio: Mongwu is the great horned owl in katsina form, and he functions as law enforcement. During the summer dances the clowns behave worse and worse - gluttony, mockery, obscenity, mimicking the audience - and everyone in the plaza can feel it building. Then Mongwu and the warriors appear on the rooftops, watch for a while, come down and thrash them. The clowns are drenched, whipped, and made to apologise. It is a set piece about excess and consequences played out over an entire afternoon in front of the whole village.
entities.variantTraditions: Owls are widely regarded with suspicion across the Southwest and are associated with witchcraft in several Pueblo traditions.

entities.name: Eototo
entities.role: The chief of all katsinam, who walks slowly and draws clouds on the ground
epithets: the spiritual counterpart of the village chief
symbols: the cloud symbols drawn in cornmeal
entities.abode: The kiva, and the plaza at Powamu and Niman
entities.bio: The most important katsina, and the plainest-looking one in the whole set.
entities.longBio: Eototo is the chief. His mask is almost featureless white - no beak, no horns, no colour to speak of - and next to the spectacular ones he looks like nobody. That is the point. He moves at a deliberate walk, stopping to draw cloud symbols on the ground in cornmeal and pour water on them, which is the single most important thing anyone in the plaza is doing. His human counterpart is the village chief, and the two are understood to be the same office in different worlds.
entities.variantTraditions: Eototo appears with his lieutenant Aholi and the pairing is fixed; Fewkes's Hopi artists drew them together.

entities.name: Aholi
entities.role: Eototo's lieutenant, in a cloak painted with flowers and clouds
epithets: the one with the long staff
entities.bio: He carries the staff and wears the best cloak, and his job is to follow the chief.
entities.longBio: Aholi walks with Eototo and repeats what he does, holding a long staff and wearing a cloak painted with clouds and flowers that is among the most striking things in the ceremony. His mask is a tall case with a crescent and a curved beak. In one account he once allowed his own throat to be cut so that Eototo could get away, which is why the cloak is coloured as it is. He is a good example of how the katsinam work in pairs and how much of the meaning is carried in the clothes rather than the face.
entities.variantTraditions: Aholi is sometimes identified with Aaloosaka, the Two Horn society deity, and the relationship between the names is unclear.

entities.name: Ahola
entities.role: The one who opens the season, going house to house at sunrise
domains: the opening of the katsina season
symbols: the mask divided in two halves
entities.abode: Every house in the village, at dawn
entities.bio: At Powamu he visits every house in the village before sunrise and marks each one.
entities.longBio: Ahola opens the great February ceremony. Before dawn he goes to every kiva and every clan house, makes a mark with cornmeal, and asks for a good year. He carries a chief's stick, moves with a peculiar stooping gait, and utters a long groaning call. At sunrise he faces the sun and bows four times. His mask is divided down the middle into two halves of different colour. Of everything in Powamu, his round of the houses at first light is the part that most sounds like what it is: someone going door to door asking for the year to work.
entities.variantTraditions: Ahola and Ahöla are the same figure; the germ-god association links him to Muyingwa.

entities.name: Crow Mother
entities.role: The mother of the katsinam, with crow wings on either side of her face
symbols: the black crow wings at the ears
entities.abode: The plaza and the kiva at Powamu
entities.bio: She carries the yucca whips to the children's initiation - and she brings the bean sprouts.
entities.longBio: Crow Mother is the mother of the katsinam and the central female figure of Powamu. She has a black crow's wing on each side of her head and carries a basket. At the initiation of children she brings the whips that the Hu katsinam use, which sounds harsh and is: the children are struck, and it is the moment they learn who the katsinam actually are. She also carries in the bean sprouts forced green in the kivas in February. Both things at once - the discipline and the growth - is exactly the point of her.
entities.variantTraditions: She is called Tumas on some mesas. Her role at the children's initiation is described in detail in Voth and is the most-cited passage of the whole Powamu literature.

entities.name: The Hu Katsinam
entities.role: The whippers: two of them, and they are the reason children find out
symbols: the black mask with staring eyes
entities.abode: The kiva at the children's initiation
entities.bio: They come into the kiva at the initiation, and afterwards the katsinam take their masks off.
entities.longBio: The Hu katsinam arrive at the initiation of children, take the whips from Crow Mother, and strike each child four times. It is real and it hurts. And then, at the end of the ceremony, the katsinam remove their masks in front of the children, who see for the first time that they are their uncles and neighbours. Accounts by Hopi people of that moment describe shock, and then a much larger understanding: the men are not pretending to be katsinam, the katsinam are present in them. Every ethnographer who recorded it understood they had been told something serious.
entities.variantTraditions: The unmasking is described from the inside in Hopi autobiographical accounts published in the twentieth century, which is how outsiders know what it meant.

entities.name: Soyoko
entities.role: The ogre woman who comes for children who have not behaved, with a knife and a basket
symbols: the crook and the long knife
the black beak and staring eyes
entities.bio: She turns up at the door with a basket to carry your children away, and the family has to buy them back.
entities.longBio: Soyoko is the single most effective piece of parenting in the ethnographic record. In February she and the Natackas go house to house naming specific children and demanding them, and the child has to come out and face her. She has a huge beak, staring eyes, a knife and a basket. The family negotiates - offering food instead, and the child is made to promise to do better - and over several visits the price is haggled up until she is finally bought off with meat. The children are genuinely frightened, the adults are visibly enjoying it, and the whole village is watching.
entities.variantTraditions: The ogre visits are still held. Photographs and detailed descriptions from the 1890s are in the published record; what is here is that material.

entities.name: Nataska
entities.role: The ogre with the black beak and the saw, who comes with her
entities.bio: He stands behind the ogre woman clacking an enormous wooden beak, which is somehow worse.
entities.longBio: The Natacka are the ogre woman's companions - large, black-beaked, carrying saws and bows, and their beaks are hinged so they can be snapped loudly. They do not do the talking. They stand at the back, working the beak, while she names the child and states the terms, and the effect of the pair is far greater than either alone. The whole performance takes place over several visits across the Powamu season, so the dread builds. It is a piece of theatre with a serious purpose and it is played expertly.
entities.variantTraditions: Natacka, Nata'aska and Nataska are the same name in different transcriptions. There are several distinct ogres in the group.

entities.name: The Mudheads
entities.role: Lumpy brown clowns with knobs on their heads, who are also drummers, announcers and priests
symbols: the brown mud-daubed mask with seven knobs
entities.bio: The most recognisable figures in the Southwest, and much more serious than they look.
entities.longBio: The Koyemsi are lumpy, brown, and covered in knobs stuffed with cotton and seeds. They organise games with the audience, hand out prizes, drum for the dancers, announce what is happening, and clown. They are also, in the Zuni account they come from, born of an incestuous union and dangerous, and are treated with real respect. In Hopi practice they turn up alongside almost any dance. If you have seen one image of a Southwestern ceremonial figure it was probably this one, and it was probably captioned wrongly.
entities.variantTraditions: The Koyemsi are Zuni in origin and were adopted by the Hopi, which is why their story and their treatment do not entirely match Hopi patterns.

entities.name: The Clowns
entities.role: Striped clowns who eat filth, mock everyone, and are publicly punished for it
symbols: the black and white horizontal stripes
entities.bio: They arrive on the roof, come down backwards, and spend the day being everything a person should not be.
entities.longBio: The clowns paint themselves in black and white stripes with two cornhusk horns, arrive by climbing down into the plaza the wrong way round, and behave appallingly for hours. They eat enormous quantities, drink filthy water, mock the audience by name, imitate visitors, and get more and more out of hand. Then the warriors and Mongwu the owl come and thrash them, and they apologise. It is not comic relief inserted into a serious ceremony. It is a lesson about immoderation delivered by demonstration, and the punishment is the second half of the argument.
entities.variantTraditions: Pueblo clowning is a serious institution with genuine authority, and the practice of naming and mocking individuals is a real form of social correction.

entities.name: Kookopolo
entities.role: The real one behind the flute-player on every fridge magnet in Arizona
symbols: the flute in the popular image
the black and white body paint
entities.abode: The plaza, and the rock walls
entities.bio: The commercialised Kokopelli is a very cleaned-up version of a figure who was frankly obscene.
entities.longBio: The hunched flute player is everywhere in the Southwest tourist trade, and the actual Kookopölö katsina is a fertility figure whose performances were explicitly sexual and often very funny - and were suppressed and sanitised after outside observers objected. The rock-art figure the logo derives from appears across the Southwest for well over a thousand years and may or may not be the same being. Almost everything printed on the merchandise is invented. The entry is here mainly so that the difference between the two is on the record.
entities.variantTraditions: The name Kokopelli is a garbling. The relationship between the katsina, the ancient petroglyph figure and the modern logo is not straightforward and is often asserted more confidently than the evidence allows.

entities.name: Hemis Katsina
entities.role: The one who closes the season, carrying the first corn of the year
symbols: the tall painted tablita above the mask
entities.abode: The plaza at Niman, in July
entities.bio: At the Home Dance in July he brings the year's first corn, and then the katsinam go home.
entities.longBio: The Hemis is the katsina of the Niman, the Home Dance, held in July. He wears a tall flat painted board above the mask - the tablita - and brings in the first green corn of the year, which is distributed. It is the last dance of the season. Afterwards the katsinam leave the villages and return to the San Francisco Peaks for six months, and the year turns to the societies' ceremonies instead. Girls who married that year receive their wedding robes at Niman. It is the closing of a door, and it is the most photographed dance because it is also the most beautiful.
entities.variantTraditions: Hemis is named for Jemez Pueblo, from which the form was borrowed. The Niman has been closed to outsiders in most villages.

entities.name: Water Drinking Girl
entities.role: The butterfly maiden of the tourist posters, who is actually about drinking water
entities.bio: The most elaborate headdress in the whole set, and the name means the girl who drinks water.
entities.longBio: Palhikmana wears a tall stepped and painted tablita covered in cloud and rain symbols, and she is a favourite subject for carvers, which is why her image is on everything. The popular name butterfly maiden comes from the whorled hairdressing, but the actual name means something closer to the maiden who drinks moisture, which is a great deal more to the point in that country. She appears in the mixed dances and is sometimes represented as a doll rather than a dancer.
entities.variantTraditions: The butterfly identification is a modern gloss. The word palhik refers to moisture.

entities.name: Chakwaina
entities.role: The fierce warrior katsina, possibly named after a member of Coronado's expedition
epithets: the black one with the beard
symbols: the black mask with a great beard of hair
entities.bio: One theory has him named for Estevanico, the enslaved African who reached the Southwest in 1539.
entities.longBio: Chakwaina is a fierce black-masked warrior katsina with a heavy beard, bulging eyes and a snapping mouth, and he appears among the Hopi, Zuni and Acoma. A long-standing suggestion connects him to Estevanico, the Moroccan-born enslaved man who guided the first Spanish reconnaissance north in 1539 and was killed at Hawikuh. Whether the connection is real is contested and probably unprovable, but the possibility that a katsina commemorates the first non-Native person the Pueblos ever met makes him worth including.
entities.variantTraditions: The Estevanico theory is popular and disputed. Chakwaina is female or a mother figure in some Zuni contexts, which complicates it further.

entities.name: Eagle Katsina
entities.role: The eagle, danced with the arms held out as wings
symbols: the eagle feather wings on the arms
entities.bio: The dance is a real imitation of an eagle, and it is one of the finest things to watch.
entities.longBio: Kwahu dances with feathered wings bound along his arms and moves like the bird - the head turns, the wings open and close, the body dips. Eagles matter enormously: young eagles are taken from nests on clan-owned cliffs, raised on the rooftops of the villages through the summer, and their feathers are used for prayer sticks. The birds are treated as guests and are sent home after Niman. The relationship is closer and more complicated than a symbol.
entities.variantTraditions: Eagle gathering is a regulated traditional practice and remains a live legal question in the United States.

entities.name: Badger Katsina
entities.role: The badger, who is the doctor - because badgers dig up roots
symbols: the black and white face markings
entities.bio: The Badger clan holds the medicine, on the straightforward grounds that badgers know where the roots are.
entities.longBio: Honan is the badger, and the Badger clan is the one that holds curing knowledge and the Powamu ceremony. The logic is entirely practical: badgers dig, digging gets you roots, roots are medicine. Katsinam of this kind - badger, bear, wolf, antelope, deer - carry the character of the animal into the plaza, and their clans hold the offices that follow from it. It is a good illustration of how Hopi ceremonial organisation and Hopi natural history are the same subject.
entities.variantTraditions: Clan ownership of specific ceremonies is the organising principle of Hopi religious life and varies between villages.

entities.name: Hahai'i Wuuti
entities.role: The talkative mother, the first doll a Hopi baby is given
symbols: the round white face with a wide smile
entities.bio: She is the flat doll hung over a baby's cradleboard, and she is the one katsina who talks a lot.
entities.longBio: Hahai'i Wuuti is a mother figure, always cheerful, with a wide painted smile, and unusually among the katsinam she speaks - a high continuous chatter. Her flat tihu is the first one given to an infant, hung on the cradleboard, and children get more elaborate carved ones as they grow. She appears with the Water Serpent ceremony pouring water, and she accompanies the ogres, where her role is to plead for the children. The carved tihu are teaching objects rather than toys, which is the thing outsiders most consistently get wrong about them.
entities.variantTraditions: The flat cradle tihu and the fully carved figures are different classes of object with different purposes.

entities.name: Dawn Woman
entities.role: Brought down the mesa by torchlight for the men's initiation
entities.bio: Her carved image is fetched at night from a shrine below the mesa and carried up by torchlight.
entities.longBio: Talatumsi is Dawn Woman, and she is represented by a carved figure kept at a shrine below the village. During the Wuwtsim initiation her image is fetched at night and carried up the mesa by men with torches, a procession that observers described as one of the most striking things they had seen. She belongs to the men's societies rather than the katsina cycle. In 1978 her figure was stolen from its shrine, which is a reminder of why Hopi people are careful about what gets published and photographed.
entities.variantTraditions: The theft of ceremonial objects from shrines is a continuing problem and is one reason many ceremonies were closed to outsiders in the twentieth century.

entities.name: Sand Altar Woman
entities.role: Mother of the katsinam and of all wild game
symbols: the sand painting on the altar
entities.bio: She owns the animals that get hunted, and is named for the sand paintings on the kiva floor.
entities.longBio: Tuwapongtumsi is Sand Altar Woman, associated with the dry paintings made in coloured sand on the kiva floor before a ceremony and destroyed after it. She is a mother of the katsinam and the owner of game animals, so hunting is petitioned through her. She is sometimes identified with or paired against Hahai'i Wuuti, and the sources do not agree about how many mother-goddesses there are or which names belong to which. That kind of ambiguity is normal here and is not a gap in the record so much as a feature of it.
entities.variantTraditions: Names and functions of the Hopi mother deities vary considerably between the three mesas.

entities.name: Longhair Katsina
entities.role: The one with the long loose hair, who sings the best songs
entities.abode: The plaza in the mixed dances
entities.bio: Long black hair down over the face, and by common consent the most beautiful singing of the year.
entities.longBio: The Longhairs dance in long lines with their hair loose over their faces, wearing spruce collars, and their songs are widely considered the finest in the repertoire - slow, low and enormously long. They are rain katsinam. New songs are composed each year, and the composing is taken as seriously as anything else. Recordings made in the early twentieth century are the reason some of this is preserved outside the villages at all, and they are also part of why Hopi people became wary of recording equipment.
entities.variantTraditions: Angak'china appear in numerous Pueblo traditions with local variations.

entities.name: Heheya
entities.role: He says everything backwards, and he is a serious rain katsina anyway
epithets: the one who speaks in reverse
symbols: the zigzag lines on the cheeks
entities.bio: Everything he says means the opposite, which is funny until you notice it is also how he asks for rain.
entities.longBio: Heheya speaks in reverse - saying the opposite of what he means, and being understood perfectly. He appears in the mixed dances and with the ogres, and his zigzag cheek markings are distinctive. Reversal as a mode is taken seriously across the Pueblos: the clown who does everything backwards, the speech that inverts, the dancer who enters the wrong way. It marks a being as standing outside ordinary rules, which is exactly the position from which you can ask for something as unreasonable as rain in that country.
entities.variantTraditions: Several distinct Heheya katsinam exist with different roles.
